review.material: MIT OCW May 18, 2015 PDF: introductory proof discussion, Chapter 4 selected sets/functions/relations definitions (pp.81–89), and §5.4 opening robot invariant example (pp.130–132) read.
review.limitations: The 920-page text and its later proofs, counting and probability chapters were not reviewed. Textbook examples illustrate mathematical reasoning; no new empirical test is reported.

State transitions and a parity invariant

sections.title: What the selected text explains
sections.text: How sets, functions, relations and proofs describe computational processes precisely. The useful connection here is between a sequence of rule applications and a mathematical transition system.

sections.title: The essential distinction
sections.text: Many successful examples do not prove a universal statement. The text’s initially promising polynomial n²+n+41 fails to be prime at n=40. A preserved invariant instead supports an argument covering every permitted step.

sections.title: Method and worked example
sections.text: Model a robot’s position as an integer pair and its moves as transitions to diagonal neighbors. The coordinate sum starts even and each move changes it by −2, 0 or 2. Consequently the robot cannot reach (1,0).

sections.title: What this gives you
sections.text: Invariants can rule out entire families of outcomes without enumerating every path. The claim concerns the stated transition model; changing the allowed moves changes the argument.

sections.title: A convention to notice
sections.text: This text allows partial functions and calls a function total when defined throughout its domain. Other introductory sources here use “function” for total functions. Check that convention before comparing definitions.
